title: How do we spot equal expressions by their terms?
description: Two sets of expressions are sorted into those with equal value without working anything out, by listing the terms of each. Expressions with the same terms have the same value.
teaching_notes: Let the child try first, then compare. One idea: list the terms with their signs and compare the lists, without working out any value. Ask the child to say why a bracket after a plus sign changes no term.

video_script.why: The child lists the terms of each expression with their signs and compares the lists, instead of working out the values.
video_script.substitution: The same method works with other numbers: write each term with its sign and compare.
video_script.anchor: two sets of expressions with the same numbers
video_script.payoff_line: Expressions with the same terms have the same value.

final_answer.value: (a) 319 − 537 and −537 + 319 are equal (b) the first three are equal, and 87 − 46 + 109 equals (87 − 46) + 109
final_answer.spoken: in the first set the second and third are equal; in the second set the first three are equal, and the fourth equals the last

maths_rules: -537 + 319 has the terms -537 and 319, the same terms as 319 - 537, so they are equal
537 - 319 has the terms 537 and -319, which match no other
87 + 46 - 109 (three times) has the terms 87, 46 and -109, so the first three are equal
87 - 46 + 109 and (87 - 46) + 109 have the terms 87, -46 and 109, so they are equal
87 - (46 + 109) = 87 - 46 - 109 has the terms 87, -46 and -109, which match no other
video_script.design: One idea: list the terms with their signs and compare, without working out any value. The two sets stay in the anchor band; the working band lists the terms. No hard clear.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, list the terms in the first set.
The first expression has the terms three hundred and nineteen and five hundred and thirty seven.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The second has the terms three hundred and nineteen and minus five hundred and thirty seven.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The third has the terms minus five hundred and thirty seven and three hundred and nineteen.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>The fourth has five hundred and thirty seven and minus three hundred and nineteen.

<bookmark mark='m2'/>The first and the fourth have terms that match no other expression.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, the first three expressions are one expression written three times.
They have the terms eighty seven, forty six and minus one hundred and nine.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The fourth and the last have the terms eighty seven, minus forty six and one hundred and nine.
<bookmark mark='m2b'/>A bracket after the first term does not change any term.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The fifth is eighty seven minus forty six minus one hundred and nine, which matches none.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, check by turning the terms round.
<bookmark mark='m1b'/>Minus five hundred and thirty seven plus three hundred and nineteen has the same two terms.
<bookmark mark='m1c'/>That matches three hundred and nineteen minus five hundred and thirty seven.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The bracket round eighty seven minus forty six can be dropped, since the plus sign follows it.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The fifth has minus one hundred and nine, but the fourth has plus one hundred and nine.
